# Google OKF in Practice: Persistent Memory and Knowledge Patterns for AI Agents

The video features the Open Knowledge Format (OKF) 0.2, a plain text format to store knowledge, and the OKF Agent Memory project, which uses the format as a persistent memory for AI agents. Explains the five-layer architecture, agent rules and commands to use on a daily basis.

Video by Maurício Yokoyama Issei, published on September 11, 2026 (9 min 21 s).
Watch: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tnS7hxUnHI4

_The video and the transcript are in Portuguese. The minutes between brackets, such as [04:12], point to the excerpt of the video._

## Amnesia of AI agents

The video deals with a common problem: the AI agent forgets the context of architecture in the middle of a code session [00:00]. The proposal is a simple text pattern, supported by Google, to give the agent a long-term memory [00:20].

During a session, the agent receives instructions, makes architectural decisions and discovers the context of the domain. When the context window closes, everything disappears [01:02]. A persistent memory layer that does not depend on a specific company [01:23] is missing.

Today, the options are bad [01:43]:

- Markdown files improvised, unstructured, that swell the context window and spend tokens [01:43].
- Vector, expensive, opaque databases that create supplier dependency [01:43].

## What is OKF

Open Knowledge Format, version 0.2, was announced by Google Cloud in June 2026 [02:25]. It is neither a software nor a database: it is an open and neutral specification [02:25]. Knowledge is in a Markdown file directory with YAML header [02:25]. The only mandatory field is `type` [02:47].

The video compares OKF to a knowledge USB-C cable: a common format that any AI can read, write and exchange without a different SDK for each project [03:07].

The design follows three principles [03:29]:

- be minimally opinative, without imposing rigid structures [03:29];
- separate who produces from who consumes: a decision written by an AI can be read months later in a common text editor [03:29];
- focus on the format, not the platform [03:49].

## The architecture

Everything stays in a knowledge bundle, which is a common directory tree [04:10]. Each concept has a Markdown file with a unique ID, metadata at the top, text body and links to other concepts [04:10]. With simple Markdown links, agents follow the knowledge network as a graph, without database [04:31].

The system has five layers [04:52]:

1. the specification of OKF [04:52];
2. the conventions of memory [04:52];
3. the skills and prompts of the agent [04:52];
4. the tools, which validate the files [04:52];
5. the knowledge of the project [05:12].

Separate the layers takes from the model the work with formatting: the tool guarantees the structure [05:12].

## The OKF agent

The OKF Agent Memory takes the format to Git as an agent's memory [05:12]. According to the video, the search takes less than 300 microseconds, with BM25 indexes, in a Go binary without external dependencies [05:33]. The project says it reduces the waste of tokens by 80% [05:54]. This comes from progressive disclosure: the IA consults the indexes and carries only the concepts it needs [06:16].

The agent follows strict rules [06:16]:

- search before writing [06:16];
- prefer updating a file to creating a duplicate [06:16];
- mark the origin of the data [06:37];
- explicitly say when you are not sure about something [06:37].

## In practice

The main commands are [06:58]:

- `okf bootstrap`, which sets the memory base of the project [06:58];
- `okf validate`, which checks if the files follow the specification [06:58];
- `okf search`, to fetch [07:19];
- `okf create`, to create a concept [07:19].

Every change in memory passes through Git and enters the normal code revision [07:19]. The `okf mcp` command rises an MCP server by default input and output without opening network port [07:39]. The context becomes private on the local machine and connects to editors such as Cursor, Codex and Claude, without network API cost [07:39].

## The Future of Knowledge

The video contrasts proprietary, fragile and opaque vector stores, with simple text knowledge packages, Git natives and auditable by anyone [08:20]. The final question is whether the organization's knowledge will be readable by the agents of the future or will be stuck in a black box [08:40].

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is OKF a database?

Nope. It is an open specification: a Markdown file directory with YAML header [02:25].

### Which field is required in an OKF concept?

Only the field `type` [02:47].

### Do I need a cloud server to use OKF memory?

Nope. According to the video, the MCP server runs on the local machine by default input and output [07:39].

- [Okf-memory/okf-agent-memory: Git-native persistent memory for AI coding agents](https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory): OKF Agent Memory is a binary without external dependencies, with BM25 memory search, bootstrap, validate, search and create commands, MCP server and five-layer architecture.

## About the video

In this explanatory video, we explore the **Google Open Knowledge Format (OKF)** and demonstrate how to use the ecosystem **okf-agent-memory** In practice!

O **OKF** is an open and vendor-neutral specification that formalizes organizational knowledge in a Markdown file structure enriched with YAML (frontmatter) metadata. It solves the fragmented context problem in AI systems, creating a navigable knowledge graph, versioned in Git and directly readable by humans and AI agents, without the need for complex vector databases.

We deepened version updates **OKF v0.2**, which introduces signs of trust, traceability of provenance (`generated`, `verified`, `sources`), life cycle management (`status`, `stale_after`) and certified computing. 

In addition, we present the ecosystem **okf-agent-memory**, developed in Go with search BM25 in high speed memory (less than 300μs) and MCP server (Model Context Protocol) embedded for direct integration with tools such as Claude Code and Cursor.
